lf~lf#1.text: The type of person that you're going to buy a company from when you have no capital to put into the deal is going to be a motivated seller, right? You need to look for a motivated seller, someone who actually wants to sell. Now you'd think this is fucking common sense but a lot of people get into acquisitions, you start talking to business owners. Let's say you're listening to me and you're not going straight to the brokers, you're actually reaching out to your target companies. Companies that fit your criteria, right? Because you need to be a disciplined deal maker if you're going to make money with deal making.

lf~lf#2.text: So let's say you go find deals yourself and you reach out to owners directly and you're having the conversation with them about buying their company.

lf~lf#3.text: Nine out of ten owners you're not going to do a deal with. That's just the nature of it. That one out of ten, the one guy who literally says I need to sell. I really want to sell. That's what's on my mind, that's my business goal, to sell this business.

lf~lf#4.text: You don't want to talk to people who are, oh yeah, yeah, I might sell. Yeah, thinking about it. Yeah, sounds nice. Yeah, you know, you don't want someone who's half -assed about it because if they are going to pull the trigger to sell their business, they're going to want cash, right? They're going to want a reason to get out of their business.

lf~lf#5.text: Now, you're probably thinking, what are you talking about?

lf~lf#6.text: If you're not going to convince people, like if you're not going to have the conversation and find out how you can do a deal, then what am I really looking for? No, I'm not looking for a fire sale. And what is a fire sale? A business is going down, you know, it's going down the toilet and the owner wants to cash out before it really hits zero, right? The owner wants to cash out 50, 100 grand, 200 grand, whatever the business might be worth as it's declining, right? That's a fire sale. That's not what I'm after.

lf~lf#7.text: I'm talking about right now, the opportunity, the silver tsunami. You've got a lot of owners, a lot of business owners in traditional industries, traditional service -based industries like healthcare that I'm in.

lf~lf#8.text: There's a lot of owners that are ready to retire,

lf~lf#9.text: but their businesses are great, they're fine. Their businesses are, you know, doing under a mill, over a mill, couple mill.

lf~lf#10.text: And this has just been supporting this person's lifestyle for the past 20 years, right? This is the type of person that you want to buy from, because they're not necessarily motivated by the money, right?

lf~lf#11.text: Money is always a big part of the conversation, but a motivated seller wants to sell the business. And it could be for whatever reason, it could be

lf~lf#12.text: their daughter's got cancer, it could be their mother's sick, it could be they want to move, they want to relocate to bloody Dubai, right? So just because someone wants to sell their business doesn't mean it's failing, right? Selling your business is a business like strategy, right? Building something up to sell.

lf~lf#13.text: Now, let's go back to the capital thing, right? The reason why I'm saying you need to speak to motivated sellers, because you're not going to do a no money down deal with a non -motivated seller, right? Someone who's not motivated to sell outside of financial gain, right? You want to look for people who are motivated to sell outside of financial gain.

lf~lf#14.text: And only these types of people will accept no money down deals. It's not only 99 .9 % of the time, it's these people.

lf~lf#15.text: People who are happy to accept money over time.

lf~lf#21.text: Most of the time is due to sentimental value.

lf~lf#22.text: And if you go into a hot industry like healthcare, chances are that these owners have spoken to some private equity, some corporate, some guy who wants to buy their business. And they have just lowballed the guy and said,

lf~lf#23.text: the guy might be doing 200 something grand in profit, and then the private equity guys would be like, yep, here's 500 grand, take it, I'll leave. And most people just leave it because in their head, they go, you're going to give me 500 grand, I make 250 grand profit,

lf~lf#24.text: I can just stay in this business for two years and get 500 grand.

lf~lf#25.text: An owner that uses that rationale doesn't understand finances. Just because you have 250K profit doesn't mean you have 250K cash at

lf~lf#26.text: the end. So what I'm saying is, these businesses are valued at what they are. But the owners have a high value on their business, usually because of sentimental reasons.

lf~lf#27.text: And, you know, I talked about deal discipline, a lot of the private equity guys, the corporate guys, they're not, they've got money they've got to throw out, right? They've got investors, they've got $100 million, they've got to get out the door. So they're not going to entertain vendor finance deals. And they've got quotas and metrics to maintain. So they're not going to necessarily overpay for businesses, especially in a traditional service based business. Overpaying is, it hurts. Because a traditional service based business, nine times out of 10, you're relying on a person, a provider, right? Someone who can actually deliver the service to deliver the service and collect the money.

lf~lf#28.text: So the valuation of a service based business is usually tied to headcount and utilization.

lf~lf#29.text: And when you value a business at a certain time, and then boom, all of a sudden, which is very, very, very common, a new owner comes into a 2030 year old business,

lf~lf#30.text: chances are a business that old has had long standing staff that are also exiting. So you've got also got to consider the fact that when you take over this business, half the staff want to leave.

lf~lf#31.text: And now this is a cost, this is going to be a cost to you in cash flow. But also, it means you're down service provided your down bodies who can actually deliver the service and collect the cash. So all of this, you have to consider in your deal structuring. And you can the perfect way to do it is to do a vendor finance deal. In other words, I call it a vendor fuck deal. Because I love the profanities. But I've done two 100 %  vendor finance deals in a in healthcare.

lf~lf#32.text: Supposedly, deal structures and a deal approach and a mentality that is impossible. You go out there most people who teach you how to buy businesses who are in acquisitions, they will say 100 % vendor finance. It is impossible, impossible. It's a scam.

lf~lf#33.text: And yeah, you create your own reality. So whatever you choose to believe, that's what your reality is.

lf~lf#34.text: Now, I'm saying this as someone who's literally done the deals, done the deals at the most, most acquirers out there say is impossible. Now, when I showed it to my billionaire mentor, I said, check out the deal that I did, my first ever deal, 100 % vendor finance, pulled out six figures cash straight away from for myself. And he goes, amazing.

lf~lf#35.text: Fantastic. I've never seen something like this before. And this is mind you, this is a guy that has a 30, 40 year career in corporate finance. So the fact that he goes to me, I've actually never seen someone pull off a deal like you.

lf~lf#36.text: That says something. I know something, right?

lf~lf#37.text: So anyway, I'll leave it at that.

lf~lf#38.text: I hope that helps. Hope that gives you a good understanding of what to look for when speaking to vendors.
